{"id": "111:1/q12", "question": "What does wa-tabba add?", "turns_on": "Whether the second verb fulfills, repeats, expands, or differently identifies the first loss.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q12/p1", "position": "It reports that Abu Lahab has perished, fulfilling the opening", "reasons": "Farra, Tabari, Wahidi, Baghawi, Razi, Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, Biqai and Qutb hear prayer followed by confirmation that it happened. Ibn Masud's wa-qad tabba marks fact; Tabari and Baydawi give ordinary Arabic and poetic parallels. Nasafi cites wa-qad fa'ala; Ibn Ashur cites al-Nabigha and Ibn Rawaha. Alusi says qad cannot introduce a curse."}, {"id": "111:1/q12/p2", "position": "It extends ruin from hands or work to the whole person", "reasons": "Muqatil, Tabari, Mawardi, Zamakhshari, Qurtubi, Ibn Jawzi, Biqai and Ibn Ashur move from ruined hands or work to the man's entire ruin; Ibn Ashur notes that the wider scope licenses waw coordination. Tabrisi says he perished in every respect."}, {"id": "111:1/q12/p3", "position": "It asserts ruin already certain by divine decree", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya and Biqai take the second clause as making the decreed loss certain; Ibn Abbas's Pen report and Hasan's Preserved Book report later illustrate prior writing, and Elmalili says the full bodily and spiritual loss endured."}, {"id": "111:1/q12/p4", "position": "Both clauses report failed deeds and personal ruin", "reasons": "Tabrisi, Razi, Baydawi and Alusi report two factual clauses: worthless deeds or what hands earned, then destruction of the person. Alusi and Biqai say past tense can assert certainty."}, {"id": "111:1/q12/p5", "position": "Both clauses are curses on hands then person", "reasons": "Mawardi, Samin, Alusi and Ibn Ashur allow both to be prayers, the first for hands and second for the whole person. Ibn Ashur says this is coordinate expansion, not identical verbal emphasis."}, {"id": "111:1/q12/p6", "position": "It predicts the ruin of his son Utbah or offspring", "reasons": "Mujahid is transmitted as saying offspring or a son perished; Razi names Utbah, recounts his spitting at the Prophet and a lion killing him en route to Syria after the Prophet's prayer, and says past tense states what God already knew."}, {"id": "111:1/q12/p7", "position": "It emphatically repeats the curse", "reasons": "Majaz cites repeated phrases and numbers elsewhere for emphasis. Mawardi reports an emphatic second curse; Corpus Coranicum prefers this and cites Paret's parallel to repeated qutila in 74:19-20."}, {"id": "111:1/q12/p8", "position": "The first loses wealth or power and the second his life", "reasons": "Abu Muslim in Razi compares losing wealth and self with 39:15. Islahi says Badr crushed Abu Lahab's political dominance and his smallpox-like death fulfilled the later personal loss."}, {"id": "111:1/q12/p9", "position": "The first concerns wealth and the second the soul", "reasons": "Tustari differentiates lost wealth in the first clause and lost soul in the second, with the rest of the sura explaining it."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q13", "question": "How does waw connect the clauses?", "turns_on": "Whether waw coordinates or introduces a circumstantial report.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q13/p1", "position": "It introduces a circumstantial clause with understood qad", "reasons": "Thalabi also mentions circumstantial waw. Nahhas supplies an understood qad or allows a direct report without it; Alusi and Ibn Ashur use Ibn Masud's explicit qad, and Ibn Ashur cites al-Nabigha and Ibn Rawaha for a fulfilled state alongside the first clause."}, {"id": "111:1/q13/p2", "position": "It coordinates distinct curses or statements", "reasons": "Thalabi says waw connects the statements; Ibn Ashur says hands and person differ in scope, allowing coordination even if both are curses. Simple identical verbal emphasis would not take waw."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q14", "question": "What variant is reported for wa-tabba?", "turns_on": "Whether qad belongs to a reported variant and what it makes explicit.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q14/p1", "position": "A reading adds qad: wa-qad tabba", "reasons": "Farra, Tabari, Nahhas, Thalabi, Mawardi, Zamakhshari, Razi, Qurtubi, Baydawi and later authors transmit wa-qad tabba from Ibn Masud, also called Abd Allah, sometimes Ubayy and al-A'mash. It expressly makes the second clause a completed report; Alusi says qad cannot lead a curse."}, {"id": "111:1/q14/p2", "position": "The received text has wa-tabba", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum prefers the received wa-tabba as the harder text and calls the expanded version a secondary clarification."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q15", "question": "What occasion prompted revelation?", "turns_on": "Which narrated incident is treated as the occasion, and whether a later prediction better fits.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q15/p1", "position": "Abu Lahab cursed the Prophet after the public warning at Safa or al-Batha", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas's accounts, preserved by Tabari, Wahidi and many others and cited as in Bukhari and Muslim, describe the Prophet summoning Quraysh at Safa or al-Batha, asking whether they trusted a warning of cavalry, then warning of punishment after the near-kin command 26:214. Abu Lahab cursed him for the summons. Some mention Safiyya and Fatima, the morning alarm, or his dust-shaking hands. Ibn Ashur says 26:214 came later and posits an earlier similar warning. Islahi accepts the episode but denies it occasioned the sura."}, {"id": "111:1/q15/p2", "position": "He raised a stone against the Prophet and was stopped", "reasons": "Accounts in Nahhas, Zamakhshari, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Bursevi, Alusi and Ibn Ashur say he lifted a stone after the warning but God prevented the attack; the episode explains naming the hands."}, {"id": "111:1/q15/p3", "position": "He rejected equality with ordinary Muslims", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says Abu Lahab asked what advantage belief gave him and rejected being equal with other Muslims; Mawardi, Qurtubi and Razi transmit it."}, {"id": "111:1/q15/p4", "position": "He rejected a warning after the miraculous meal for his uncles", "reasons": "Muqatil describes Ali preparing sheep and milk for thirty-nine; Abu Lahab called the miraculous feeding sorcery, a second meal followed, and the Prophet announced his warning. Zajjaj and Razi give variants, with questions about equal Muslim reward."}, {"id": "111:1/q15/p5", "position": "His abuse of visiting delegations grieved the Prophet", "reasons": "Ibn Kaysan says he labelled the Prophet liar, magician or mad to visiting delegations; one group persisted, Abu Lahab abused him again, the Prophet grieved and revelation came. Mawardi, Razi and Qurtubi preserve it."}, {"id": "111:1/q15/p6", "position": "He mocked the afterlife and empty hands after the boycott", "reasons": "Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Abbas, Durr and Alusi recount his rejection of resurrection after the three-year boycott, support of al-Lat and al-Uzza, and gesture of blowing or looking at empty hands; the sura followed in those reports."}, {"id": "111:1/q15/p7", "position": "His wife scattered thorns on the Prophet's path", "reasons": "Ibn Hisham and Suyuti-Lubab connect revelation to Umm Jamil scattering thorns on the Prophet's path."}, {"id": "111:1/q15/p8", "position": "He tore a miraculous speaking goat kid's hands", "reasons": "Razi alone reports that a kid goat miraculously praised the Prophet, Abu Lahab tore its hands, and the curse followed."}, {"id": "111:1/q15/p9", "position": "His hostile dominance was about to end near Badr", "reasons": "Islahi rejects the notion of a retaliatory early Meccan curse; he reads certain future political defeat near Badr, after the truth was fully conveyed and before Abu Lahab's death."}]}
{"id": "111:1/q16", "question": "Could Abu Lahab still believe if his doom was decreed?", "turns_on": "How divine foreknowledge and a threat of fire leave room for commanded faith and choice.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q16/p1", "position": "His ruin was written beforehand and he could not escape it", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas says the first Pen wrote Abu Lahab's doom; Hasan says the Preserved Book fixed it before Abu Lahab and his parents existed. Qurtubi adduces the Adam-Moses exchange for prior decree; Abu Hurayra's transmissions give two thousand or forty years before Adam for the Torah's writing."}, {"id": "111:1/q16/p2", "position": "Faith remained obligatory and the threat was conditional on unbelief", "reasons": "Tabataba'i reports al-Majma's answer that belief remains obligatory and the threat applies if he dies an unbeliever. He says God's decisive decree wills human acts as voluntary, so choice persists; Alusi reports the conditional threat formulation."}, {"id": "111:1/q16/p3", "position": "He need only affirm the message generally, not every prediction", "reasons": "Alusi reports an answer distinguishing required general belief in the Prophet from assent to every Quranic prediction about oneself."}, {"id": "111:1/q16/p4", "position": "Hell does not itself prove lifelong unbelief", "reasons": "Alusi reports that Hell may punish a sinful believer, so a threat of fire alone need not prove perpetual disbelief; he says this does not solve the case of unbelievers addressed in al-Kafirun."}, {"id": "111:1/q16/p5", "position": "Another kalam answer was offered then rejected without its argument here", "reasons": "Alusi names al-Ka'bi, Abu al-Husayn al-Basri and Qadi Abd al-Jabbar as offering another answer rejected by the Imam, but gives no details and refers readers elsewhere."}]}

{"id": "111:1/q18", "question": "What does the verse teach about kinship, standing, and conduct?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q18/p1", "position": "Opposing the Prophet leads to ruin", "reasons": "Sulami's Abu Bakr ibn Tahir calls not knowing Muhammad's prophetic worth manifest loss; Qushayri says wealth cannot help an opponent. {"id": "111:1/q19", "question": "Why does this sura speak directly without saying 'say'?", "turns_on": "Why direct divine speech is used in place of a command to the Prophet.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q19/p1", "position": "God answers because the insult targeted Muhammad", "reasons": "Razi distinguishes al-Kafirun, where the unbelievers attacked God and Muhammad was told to reply, from this attack on Muhammad that God answered Himself. {"id": "111:1/q27", "question": "What objections about figurative, ambiguous, or repeated Quranic wording cite this verse?", "turns_on": "Whether such figures are defects or ordinary intelligible Arabic usage.", "positions": [{"id": "111:1/q27/p1", "position": "Critics challenge figurative and ambiguous expressions, repetition, and apparent form", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba reports critics objecting to ambiguous guidance, implied omissions, added or reversed words, metaphor, inversion, kinaya here and in 25:28, repetition, and form differing from intended meaning."}, {"id": "111:1/q27/p2", "position": "Ibn Qutayba says he answers those objections and defends known identifying names", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says he has answered those objections and others and kept unusual vocabulary in another book; he defends identifying labels against literalist objections and explains Arabs' auspicious or ugly names as omens."}]}
